Atom economy measures how much of the mass of the starting materials ends up in the product you actually want. Section 16.3 (principle 2) gives the formula as

\(\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{\text{Formula weight of the desired product}}{\text{sum of formula weight of all the reactants used in the reaction}} \times 100\)

The numerator counts only the **desired** product, so whatever mass leaves the reaction as by-product lowers the value. A good atom economy therefore means most atoms of the reactants have been incorporated into the desired product and only small amounts of unwanted by-products are formed.

The \(\gamma\)-isomer of benzene hexachloride (BHC) is called **gammexane**, also known as **lindane**.

Section 16.3 (principle 3, Less hazardous chemical synthesis) states it in these words: "Nowadays benzene hexachloride (BHC) is used as insecticide. One of the \(\Upsilon\)-isomer (gamma) of BHC is called gammexane or lindane." It is used as an insecticide in place of DDT, which was found to be harmful to living things.

\(1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\)

Section 16.5 (c. Why Nano ?) states: "One nanometer is one billionth of a meter. (that is \(1\ \mathrm{nm} = 10^{-9}\ \mathrm{m}\))." The same section defines the nanometre scale conventionally as \(1\text{–}100\ \mathrm{nm}\), which is the size range in which a material starts to show optical, structural, thermal, catalytic, magnetic and electrical properties different from those of the bulk.

**(i) Green chemistry :** Green chemistry is the use of chemistry for pollution prevention by environmentally conscious design of chemical products and processes that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances (section 16.1). Put more simply, it is an approach to chemistry that aims to maximize efficiency and minimize hazardous effects on human health and the environment. The concept was coined by Paul T. Anastas, who also enunciated its twelve principles.

**(ii) Sustainable development :** Sustainable development is development that meets the needs of the present, without compromising the ability of future generations to meet their own need (section 16.2). It has continued to evolve as protecting the world's resources, and the chapter notes that sustainable development can be achieved by adopting the twelve principles of green chemistry.

Section 16.4 sets out the role of green chemistry as follows.

1. **It works within the Earth's own capacity.** The green chemistry approach recognizes that the Earth does have a natural capacity for dealing with much of the waste and pollution that society generates; it is only when that capacity is exceeded that we become unsustainable.

2. **It promotes cleaner technology.** It promotes innovative chemical technologies that reduce or eliminate the use or generation of hazardous substances in the design, manufacture and use of chemical products.

3. **It prevents pollution rather than treating it.** Green chemistry helps to reduce capital expenditure and to prevent pollution. It incorporates pollution prevention practices in the manufacture of chemicals and promotes pollution prevention and industrial ecology.

4. **It is a new way of designing chemicals and processes.** It is a new way of looking at chemicals and their manufacturing process so as to minimize any negative environmental effects.

5. **It protects the global environment.** Green chemistry helps to protect the presence of ozone in the stratosphere, which is essential for the survival of life on the earth, and it is useful in controlling the green house effect (global warming).

Taken together, these make green chemistry the tool through which sustainable development — meeting present needs without depriving future generations — is actually put into practice.

**a. XRD** — X-ray Diffraction (the instrument is the X-ray diffractometer).

**b. TEM** — Transmission Electron Microscope; the technique is transmission electron microscopy.

**c. STM** — Scanning Tunneling Microscope.

**d. FTIR** — Fourier Transform Infrared spectroscopy (the instrument is the Fourier transform infrared spectrophotometer).

**e. SEM** — Scanning Electron Microscope; the technique is scanning electron microscopy.

Four of the five are expanded in Table 16.1 of section 16.7.3, which also records what each one measures: XRD gives particle size, crystal structure and geometry; SEM gives the structure of the surface of the material, that is its morphology; TEM gives particle size; and FTIR gives absorption by functional groups and binding nature. STM is expanded in the "Do you know ?" box of section 16.8, which notes that its invention in 1980 led to the discovery of fullerenes in 1986.

**a. Nanoscience :** Nanoscience is the study of phenomena and manipulation of materials at atomic, molecular and macromolecular scales, where properties differ significantly from those at a larger scale (section 16.5 a).

**b. Nanotechnology :** Nanotechnology is the design, characterization, production and application of structures, devices and systems by controlling shape and size at the nanometer scale (section 16.5 b).

**c. Nanomaterial :** A nanomaterial is a material having structural components with at least one dimension in the nanometer scale, that is \(1\text{–}100\ \mathrm{nm}\) (section 16.5 d). Nanomaterials are larger than single atoms but smaller than bacteria and cells, and may be nanoparticles, nanowires or nanotubes according to their dimensions.

**d. Nanochemistry :** Nanochemistry is the combination of chemistry and nanoscience. It deals with the designing and synthesis of materials of nanoscale with different size, shape, structure and composition, and their organization into functional architectures (section 16.5 e). It is used in chemical, physical and materials science as well as in engineering, biological and medical applications.

Section 16.9 (c) explains the role of nanotechnology in water purification.

Water contains waterborne pathogens such as viruses and bacteria, and the chapter records that 1.1 billion people are without access to an improved water supply, so providing safe drinking water is currently a high priority.

The nanotechnology answer is a **cost-effective filter material coated with silver nanoparticles (AgNps)**, used for example in a domestic water purifier. The silver nanoparticles act as a highly effective bacterial disinfectant and remove *E. coli* from the water.

This works because of a property described in section 16.6.2 — a nanoparticle has a very high surface-to-volume ratio, so the same mass of silver spread over the filter presents an enormously larger reactive surface to the water passing through it than bulk silver would.

Sunscreen contains **nanoparticles of zinc oxide, \(\mathrm{ZnO}\), and titanium dioxide, \(\mathrm{TiO_2}\)**.

**Use :** these chemicals protect the skin against harmful UV (ultraviolet) rays by absorbing or reflecting the light, and so prevent the skin from damage. The chapter gives this in the "Do you know ?" box of section 16.6, where it is named as a simple skin-care application of nanochemistry in medicine. (The same two oxides are named again in section 16.6.3 as photocatalysts.)

This is principle 5 of green chemistry, "Use safer solvent and auxiliaries" (section 16.3). It says : choose the safest solvent available for any given step of a reaction, and minimize the total amount of solvents and auxiliary substances used, since these make up a large percentage of the total waste created.

The chapter illustrates it as follows. The aim is to use **green solvents** — for example **water** or **supercritical \(\mathrm{CO_2}\)** — in place of volatile halogenated organic solvents such as \(\mathrm{CH_2Cl_2}\), \(\mathrm{CHCl_3}\) and \(\mathrm{CCl_4}\), for chemical synthesis and other purposes. Water is a safe and benign solvent, whereas dichloromethane is hazardous.

The reasons given for the principle are that the use of toxic solvents affects millions of workers every year and has implications for consumers and the environment as well; that many solvents are used in high volumes and many are volatile organic compounds, so their use creates large amounts of waste, air pollution and other health impacts; and that finding safer, more efficient alternatives, or removing the solvent altogether, is one of the best ways to improve a process or a product.

**Catalyst :** a catalyst is a substance which alters the rate of a chemical reaction while itself remaining chemically unchanged at the end of the reaction. This chapter does not print a formal definition; what it gives is a functional one, in principle 9 (Use of catalysis, section 16.3) — "Use of catalyst in the chemical reaction speeds up its rate. Catalyst helps to increase selectivity, minimize waste and reduce reaction times and energy demands." That is why catalysis is itself one of the twelve principles of green chemistry.

**Two examples, both named in this chapter (section 16.6.3) :**

1. **Palladium (\(\mathrm{Pd}\)) and platinum (\(\mathrm{Pt}\)) nanoparticles**, used in hydrogenation reactions.

2. **Titanium dioxide (\(\mathrm{TiO_2}\)) and zinc oxide (\(\mathrm{ZnO}\))**, used in photocatalysis.

The same section adds a third: gold in bulk form is unreactive, but gold nanoparticles are found to be very good catalysts for various organic reactions. It also explains why nanoparticles make good catalysts — surface area increases as particle size decreases, and these catalysts are heterogeneous, so the reaction occurs on the catalyst surface; the catalyst can then be separated easily and recycled.

(Note : the "Complete the chart" table printed under principle 9 lists five reactions — hydrogenation of oil, Haber's process, manufacture of HDPE, the contact process and the Fischer-Tropsch process — but leaves the catalyst column blank for the student to fill in, so the chapter itself names no catalyst there.)

Section 16.3 lists twelve principles of green chemistry, enunciated by Paul Anastas. Any three may be explained; three are given here.

**1. Prevention of waste or by-products.** Priority is given to preventing waste rather than to cleaning up and treating waste after it has been created. The chapter illustrates this with zero waste technology (ZWT), in which the waste from a chemical synthesis should be zero or a minimum, and in which the waste of one system is used as the raw material of another — for example, the bottom ash of a thermal power station can be used as raw material by the cement and brick industry, and the effluent from cleaning machinery parts may be used as coolant water in a thermal power station.

**2. Less hazardous chemical synthesis (principle 3).** Chemical reactions and synthetic routes should be designed to be as safe as possible, so that the formation of hazardous waste from chemical processes is avoided. The chapter's illustration is the insecticide DDT (dichlorodiphenyl trichloroethane), which controlled typhoid- and malaria-carrying mosquitoes effectively but was realized to be harmful to living things; benzene hexachloride (BHC), whose \(\gamma\)-isomer is gammexane or lindane, is used in its place.

**3. Design for energy efficiency (principle 6).** Chemical synthesis should be designed so as to minimize the use of energy; it is better to carry out reactions at room temperature and pressure. This can be achieved by using a proper catalyst, by using micro-organisms for organic synthesis and by using renewable materials. The chapter's illustration is that a biocatalyst can work at ambient conditions, that refluxing conditions require less energy, and that the heating technology itself can be improved, for example by microwave heating.

**Atom economy** (principle 2 of green chemistry, section 16.3) is a measure of the amount of atoms from the starting materials that are present in the useful products at the end of a chemical process. Good atom economy means most of the atoms of the reactants are incorporated into the desired product and only small amounts of unwanted by-products are formed, so there is less of a waste-disposal problem. It is calculated as

\(\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{\text{Formula weight of the desired product}}{\text{sum of formula weight of all the reactants used in the reaction}} \times 100\)

**Example (the chapter's own) — conversion of butan-1-ol to 1-bromobutane :**

\(\mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2OH} + \mathrm{NaBr} + \mathrm{H_2SO_4} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH_3CH_2CH_2CH_2\text{-}Br} + \mathrm{NaHSO_4} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

The desired product is 1-bromobutane, \(\mathrm{C_4H_9Br}\), so the numerator is the mass of \((4\mathrm{C} + 9\mathrm{H} + 1\mathrm{Br})\) atoms \(= 4(12) + 9(1) + 80 = 137\ \mathrm{u}\).

The three reactants together supply \((4\mathrm{C} + 12\mathrm{H} + 5\mathrm{O} + 1\mathrm{Br} + 1\mathrm{Na} + 1\mathrm{S})\) atoms \(= 4(12) + 12(1) + 5(16) + 80 + 23 + 32 = 275\ \mathrm{u}\).

\(\% \text{ atom economy} = \dfrac{137\ \mathrm{u}}{275\ \mathrm{u}} \times 100 = 49.81\ \%\)

So barely half the mass of the starting materials ends up in the wanted product; the remaining \(138\ \mathrm{u}\) leaves as \(\mathrm{NaHSO_4}\) and \(\mathrm{H_2O}\). A reaction with a low atom economy such as this one is wasteful even if its percentage yield is high, which is exactly the point the principle makes.

"Minimization of steps" is principle 8 of green chemistry, printed in section 16.3 as "Reduce derivatives : [Minimization of steps]". A commonly used technique in organic synthesis is the use of a protecting or blocking group; the principle says that unnecessary derivatization — installing and then removing a protecting group — should be minimized or avoided if possible, because such steps require additional reagents and generate waste.

**The chapter's illustration — synthesis of m-hydroxybenzoic acid from m-hydroxybenzaldehyde :**

1. **Protection.** The phenolic \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group of m-hydroxybenzaldehyde \(\left(\mathrm{HO\text{-}C_6H_4\text{-}CHO}\right)\) is protected as its benzyl ether using benzyl chloride, \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2Cl}\), giving \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2O\text{-}C_6H_4\text{-}CHO}\). This step is needed only because the free \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group would otherwise be attacked in the next step.

2. **The wanted step.** The \(\mathrm{-CHO}\) group is oxidised, \([\mathrm{O}]\), to \(\mathrm{-COOH}\), giving \(\mathrm{C_6H_5CH_2O\text{-}C_6H_4\text{-}COOH}\).

3. **Deprotection.** The benzyl protecting group is removed to release the \(\mathrm{-OH}\) group again, giving the product m-hydroxybenzoic acid, \(\mathrm{HO\text{-}C_6H_4\text{-}COOH}\).

Only step 2 changes the molecule into the target. Steps 1 and 3 cancel each other out — they put a group on and take the same group off — yet each consumes reagents and produces waste. As the chapter notes, in such cases the atom economy is also less. The green chemistry principle therefore aims to develop a methodology in which these unnecessary steps are avoided; where it is practicable, biocatalytic reactions very often need no protection of a selective group at all, and the aldehyde could be oxidised directly in one step.

[Textbook note (not an error): section 16.7.2 states that the sol-gel process "includes four steps : hydrolysis, polycondensation, drying and thermal decomposition", and then sets the same process out as a FIVE-item numbered list - the extra item being step 3, aging of the gel. Both are reproduced below, since a student answering this question from the chapter can legitimately arrive at either count.]

**Sol :** sols are dispersions of colloidal particles in a liquid, the colloids being solid particles with diameters of \(1\text{–}100\ \mathrm{nm}\) (section 16.7.2).

**Gel :** a gel is an interconnected rigid network with pores of submicrometer dimensions and polymeric chains whose average length is greater than a micrometer.

**The sol-gel method.** The sol-gel process is based on inorganic polymerization reactions. It is generally carried out at room temperature and is widely employed to prepare oxide materials. The chapter describes it as including four stages — hydrolysis, polycondensation, drying and thermal decomposition — and writes the two reactions involved as

\(\mathrm{MOR} + \mathrm{H_2O} \longrightarrow \mathrm{MOH} + \mathrm{ROH}\quad\text{(hydrolysis)}\)

where \(\mathrm{MOR}\) is the metal alkoxide, and

\(\mathrm{MOH} + \mathrm{ROM} \longrightarrow \mathrm{M\text{-}O\text{-}M} + \mathrm{ROH}\quad\text{(condensation)}\)

It then sets the procedure out in five numbered steps :

1. Formation of a different stable solution of the alkoxide or solvated metal precursor.

2. Gelation, resulting from the formation of an oxide- or alcohol-bridged network (the gel) by a polycondensation reaction.

3. Aging of the gel — during this period the gel transforms into a solid mass.

4. Drying of the gel, in which water and other volatile liquids are removed from the gel network.

5. Dehydration, in which the material is heated at temperatures up to \(800\ ^\circ\mathrm{C}\).

Depending on how the gel is treated, the product can be obtained as a thin film coating, as a powder or as a dense ceramic, as shown in Fig. 16.7.

The **lotus** (*Nelumbo nucifera*) is the example of self cleaning.

Section 16.9 (d) explains it : although the lotus plant grows in muddy water, its leaves always appear clean, because the leaves are superhydrophobic. Nanostructures on the lotus leaves repel water, which then carries the dirt away with it as it rolls off. This "lotus effect" is the basis of self cleaning windows.
